'''''Grevillea baueri''''', commonly known as '''Bauer's grevillea''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Makinson |first1=Robert O. |title=''Grevillea baueri'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Grevillea~baueri |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Proteaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to the coastal ranges of south-eastern New South Wales. It is a low, spreading to erect shrub with mostly oblong to egg-shaped leaves with red to pink and cream-coloured or yellow flowers.

==Description==
''Grevillea baueri'' is a low, spreading to erect shrub that typically grows to a height of up to {{cvt|0.3–1.5|m}}. Its leaves are [[Leaf#Divisions of the blade|simple]], oblong to egg-shaped, {{cvt|10–30|mm}} long and {{cvt|3–15|mm}} wide with the edges turned down or rolled under, the lower surface more or less [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]]. The flowers are arranged in groups of eight to eighteen near the ends of branches or in leaf axils on a [[rachis]] {{cvt|2–5|mm}} long, and are red to pink and cream-coloured to yellow near the tip, with a red [[Style (botany)|style]]. The [[Gynoecium#Pistils|pistil]] is usually {{cvt|16–23|mm}} long, the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] covered with long hairs. Flowering mainly occurs in winter and spring and the fruit is a hairy [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]] {{cvt|13–14|mm}} long.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="FoA">{{cite web |last1=Makinson |first1=Robert O. |title=''Grevillea baueri'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Grevillea%20baueri |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref><ref name = wrigley>{{cite book|author1=Wrigley, J.W. |author2=Fagg, M.| title=Banksias, Waratahs & Grevilleas| publisher=Collins|location= Australia | year=1989 | isbn=0-7322-0020-2}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Grevillea baueri'' was first formally described in 1810 by botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in ''[[Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Grevillea baueri''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/536434|publisher=APNI|access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref><ref name="R.Br.">{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Robert |title=On the Proteaceae of Jussieu |journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London |date=1810 |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=173 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13720#page/181/mode/1up |access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref> The specific epithet honours brothers [[Franz Bauer|Franz]] and [[Ferdinand Bauer]] who were both noted botanical illustrators from [[Austria]].<ref name = wrigley/>

In 1986, [[Donald McGillivray (botanist)|Donald McGillivray]] described two subspecies of ''G. baueri'' and the names are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:

==Distribution and habitat==
Subspecies ''asperula'' grows in heath or open woodland from near [[Nerriga]] to near [[Nowra]] and the northern edge of the [[Budawang Range]] and subsp. ''baueri'' is found in woodland and heath between [[Camden, New South Wales|Camden]], [[Picton, New South Wales|Picton]], [[Mittagong]] and [[Bundanoon]] in the coastal ranges of south-eastern New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS1" /><ref name="FoA1" /><ref name="RBGS2" /><ref name="FoA2" />

==Conservation status==
''Grevillea baueri'' is listed as [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]] on the [[IUCN Red List of Threatened Species]].  It has a limited distribution which is likely severely fragmented and the number of mature individuals, as well as the quality and extent of habitat are declining.<ref name="IUCN">{{cite iucn |author=Olde, P. |author2=Makinson, R. |year=2020 |title=''Grevillea baueri'' |volume=2020 |article-number=e.T112647029A113309225 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2020-3.RLTS.T112647029A113309225.en |access-date=21 December 2023}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
This species has attractive foliage and flowers although the latter blacken after maturity, which can detract from the overall appearance. It is frost hardy in Australia and preferes a position with reasonable drainage and in full sun or partial shade. Plants are propagated by cuttings.<ref name = wrigley/>
